verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Jalandhar sports-goods exporters with clean dealer receivables and scheme-backed capex; avoid pure domestic-seasonal units with stretched inventory.
title: Jalandhar sports goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Jalandhar's sports goods units convert rubber, leather, synthetic and wood inputs into bats, balls, shoes and gym equipment, and cash comes back through dealer and export channels, not at the factory gate.** The working-capital cycle is the whole credit story: a rated peer held inventory of ~85 days and collected from dealers in ~89 days as on March 31, 2024 [8], so when a proposal lands, check the inventory-plus-receivable days against these two numbers; if receivables run past 90 days, ask which dealers are being carried and why. Pricing power is thin — a rated peer showed limited ability to pass on costs in a sluggish market [9] — so margin is made on cost control, not price.

## What has changed now
**The local news is about intent and money, not yet about orders.** A sitting MP has publicly called for revival of the Jalandhar sports goods industry [1], and Jalandhar plus Meerut are reported to get about Rs 150 crore extra under Mission Olympic for sports goods [2]. Separately, a Centre scheme of Rs 1,857 crore is reported to boost the Jalandhar and Ludhiana industry [3]. Treat all three as local press, dated late October 2026, and unverified against sanction letters — so when a borrower cites scheme money, ask for the sanction order, not the newspaper. The data pack gives Punjab GST collections +9.7% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D], a real local tailwind, but India-wide bank credit is +26.8% YoY against output +3.8% [D], meaning much of the lending is not yet backed by production.

## Where to grow
**Pursue exporters and scheme-linked capex borrowers, not festive-season domestic fillers.** India-wide exports are +32.5% Apr-to-date in USD [D], and the peer set shows demand holding: Campus Activewear grew revenue 12.2% with volume 11.7% in Q1 FY27 [6], and Page Industries improved net working capital days from 75 to 54 [5]. So when a proposal lands, favour units with export order books and a capex plan tied to the Mission Olympic or Centre scheme [2][3]; if the borrower is purely domestic and sells into one festive season, ask for the last three years' monthly sales pattern before sanctioning.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the cycle, not the story.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, and set a drawing-power limit at 75% of eligible receivables under 90 days, consistent with the peer collection norm [8]. Ask for the scheme sanction letter and disbursement schedule before releasing capex tranches [2][3]. Peer margins are compressing — Page revenue rose 7.9% with margins down [5] — so price the limit for a margin squeeze, not for the FY26 peak.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the cash conversion, not the order book.** If inventory days cross 85 [8] or receivables cross 90 [8], cut the limit and ask for dealer-wise ageing. If scheme money is cited but no sanction letter appears within 60 days [2][3], treat the capex as unfunded. If monthly GST on the borrower's own filings lags the Punjab +9.7% trend [D], the unit is losing share.
